I’ll read the note and the repository’s research instructions, then explain how the formalism’s conditions relate to RH.

The note has two main routes: a positivity condition across the complex spectral plane that is exactly equivalent to RH, and real-variable sign conditions that exclude positive-time zero collisions. The quaternion equations organize the quantities involved; the required signs are still the open part.

The domains matter: the collision test covers real \(x\) at every positive time, while the curvature test covers every complex \(z\) at time zero. In quaternion notation, the first becomes \(f(t,x)\ne0\). The second uses \(|H|^2\); the note’s polynomial example shows why convexity of the total norm \(|f|^2\) is insufficient.

Yes. The [note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/20_constrained_operator_squares/brainstorm/03_QUATERNION_CONTINUATION_20261014.md:131) compresses two different routes to RH: **excluding positive-time zero collisions**, and **proving a curvature sign throughout the complex spectral plane**. The quaternion equations organize the relevant quantities, but establishing those signs remains open.

Start with the normalization
\[
H(0,z)=\frac18\xi\!\left(\frac12+\frac{iz}{2}\right).
\]
Real \(z\) corresponds to the critical line, so RH means precisely that every zero of \(H(0,z)\) is real.

With your quaternion state
\[
f=H+\mathbf jH_z,
\]
a zero of \(H\) need not be a zero of \(f\): at a simple zero, the derivative component remains nonzero. Thus the distinction between scalar zeros and quaternion zeros matters.

**The collision route gives an exact criterion directly in quaternion notation:**
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{RH}\iff
f(t,x)\ne0\quad\text{for every real }x\text{ and every }t>0.}
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\boxed{|f(t,x)|^2=H(t,x)^2+H_x(t,x)^2>0
\quad(t>0,\ x\in\mathbb R).}
\]

Here \(f=0\) means \(H=H_x=0\), a multiple real zero. For the genuine theta family, the manuscript’s collision reduction shows that failure of RH forces such a zero at a positive threshold time. Conversely, RH excludes positive-time multiple zeros because the local heat evolution would produce nonreal zeros just before the collision. This reduction uses the theta flow’s established threshold, localization, and local zero-splitting results; it does not follow from the quaternion equation alone. See the [manuscript’s endpoint criterion](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/20_constrained_operator_squares/manuscript/constrained_operator_squares.tex:218) and its [Polymath inputs](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.12438v2).

The strict restriction \(t>0\) is important: this criterion permits multiple zeros at time zero, as RH itself does.

The note proposes proving this nonvanishing through two **stationary sign conditions**, on real \(t,x\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_x=0&\ \Longrightarrow\
\mathscr L_0=H_x^2-HH_{xx}=-HH_{xx}\ge0,\\
H_{xx}=0&\ \Longrightarrow\
\mathscr L_1=H_{xx}^2-H_xH_{xxx}=-H_xH_{xxx}\ge0.
\end{aligned}
\]

Their meaning becomes clearer along a moving stationary point. Write \(h_j=\partial_x^jH\), and suppose \(x_j(t)\) satisfies \(\partial_xh_j(t,x_j(t))=0\). The heat equation gives
\[
\frac12\frac{d}{dt}
\bigl[h_j(t,x_j(t))^2\bigr]
=\mathscr L_j(t,x_j(t)).
\]
So these signs say that the squared stationary values of \(H\) and \(H_x\) cannot decrease as Newman time increases.

A prospective collision forces one of those stationary values to decrease to zero immediately before the collision:

- An even-multiplicity zero is detected by the condition for \(H\).
- An odd-multiplicity zero of order at least three is detected by the condition for \(H_x\).

That is why both levels appear. The signs must hold on neighborhoods **before** every possible positive-time collision. Checking only the collision point accomplishes little: both Laguerre expressions vanish there.

In quaternion language, these are signs of particular components:
\[
\overline f\,f_z=(\text{complex component})-\mathbf j\mathscr L_0,
\qquad
\overline{f_z}\,f_{zz}
=(\text{complex component})-\mathbf j\mathscr L_1.
\]
On the real slice, the required conditions control their signed \(\mathbf j\)-coefficients. Taking a norm discards that sign.

The weaker alternative allows
\[
\mathscr L_j\ge-C_j|f|^2
\quad\text{when }\partial_xh_j=0,\qquad j=0,1,
\]
provided \(C_j\ge0\) stays locally bounded through every candidate collision. Near a collision, the responsible ratio \(-\mathscr L_j/|f|^2\) diverges like \(1/(T-t)\). A bounded allowance therefore still excludes the collision. Merely defining \(C_j\) by that ratio would not prove the needed boundedness.

**The whole-plane route is a different exact criterion, imposed at time zero:**
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{RH}\iff
\mathcal C_0(0,z)
=|H_z|^2-\operatorname{Re}(H_{zz}\overline H)
\ge0\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathbb C.}
\]
Since
\[
\mathcal C_0(0,x+iy)
=\frac12\partial_y^2|H(0,x+iy)|^2,
\]
this says that the scalar squared modulus is convex along **every vertical spectral line**. This is the classical complex Laguerre criterion in the theta function’s growth class. [Csordas–Escassut, Theorem 2.4](https://www.numdam.org/item/AMBP_2005__12_2_331_0.pdf).

Its sufficiency has a simple geometric explanation. A nonreal zero \(a+ib\) would have a reflected zero \(a-ib\). The nonnegative convex function \(y\mapsto|H(0,a+iy)|^2\) would then vanish throughout the interval between them, contradicting the identity theorem.

Here the observation must be \(|H|^2\). The note’s control \(H=z^2-2t+1\) has nonreal zeros at time zero, although the total quaternion norm satisfies
\[
\frac12\partial_y^2|f|^2=2x^2+6y^2+2>0.
\]

Thus the quaternion research task is to obtain a theta-specific identity controlling either the **stationary signed components**, their **bounded negative loss**, or the **scalar vertical curvature**. The heat/Fueter identities provide the formalism; the required estimate would supply the RH argument.

Your convention concern is right: the old field is annihilated by the conjugate of the usual left Fueter operator. The RH domain is the half-plane \(q=t+\mathbf jx\), with \(t>0\) and \(x\) real.

I found useful exact simplifications. The heat evolution becomes \(F_t=-\partial_q^2F\) on the Fueter-regular field, and the Cauchy–Fueter formula reconstructs the required jets from boundary values. I’ve adopted the Fueter-regular version with **time kept independent**:
\[
F(t,q)=H(t+\overline{z_1},z_0)
+\mathbf jH_z(t+\overline{z_1},z_0),
\qquad q=z_0+\mathbf jz_1.
\]
At real quaternion arguments, it recovers \(F(t,x)=H(t,x)+\mathbf jH_x(t,x)\). Thus your compact statement is correct for this explicitly defined lift:
\[
\boxed{\mathrm{RH}\iff F(t,x)\ne0
\quad\text{for every }t>0,\ x\in\mathbb R.}
\]
Its Fueter regularity holds unconditionally; nonvanishing is the RH content.

I also investigated the integral formulas and found several useful reformulations, saved in [the new research note](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-2/active/21_quaternion_theta_geometry/notes/4_CAUCHY_FUETER_BOUNDARY_AND_CURRENT_REFORMULATIONS_20261014.md).

The evolution becomes the compact system
\[
\boxed{\bar\partial_qF=0,\qquad
\partial_tF=-\partial_q^{\,2}F,}
\]
where \(\partial_q\) is the normalized conjugate Fueter operator. Its iterates recover the entire derivative hierarchy.

The Cauchy–Fueter formula reconstructs the field—and, by differentiation, its jets—from boundary values:
\[
F(t,q)=\int_{\partial\Omega}
\frac{\overline{p-q}}{2\pi^2|p-q|^4}\,
n(p)F(t,p)\,dS_p.
\]
The multiplication order matters. This is the standard left-regular formula. [Frenkel–Libine, Theorem 9](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0711.2699).

Writing \(A_m=\partial_q^mF(t,x)\), the two Laguerre observations become
\[
\mathscr L_0=\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf j\overline{A_0}A_1),
\qquad
\mathscr L_1=\operatorname{Re}(\mathbf j\overline{A_1}A_2).
\]
Consequently, both admit exact **signed boundary-correlation formulas**. The note gives particularly simple spherical moment versions.

There is also a useful simplification of the proof target. For
\(\mathcal E=|F(t,x)|^2\),
\[
H_x=0\Rightarrow\mathcal E_t=2\mathscr L_0,
\qquad
H_{xx}=0\Rightarrow\mathcal E_t=2\mathscr L_1.
\]
Thus both stationary signs combine into
\[
\boxed{\mathcal E_t\ge0\quad\text{where }H_xH_{xx}=0.}
\]
The bounded-loss version combines similarly.

I obtained a **bounded theta-specific estimate** for the physical Fueter field \(F(t,x)=H(t,x)+\mathbf jH_x(t,x)\):

\[

\qquad(0\le t\le1,\ |x|\le8).}

The proof includes the complete theta series and integration tail. Its key inequality is
\[
M_2(t)-\frac{25}{2}M_4(t)>\frac1{120000},
\qquad
M_k(t)=\int_0^\infty u^k e^{tu^2}\Phi(u)\,du.
\]
This also gives \(H_{xx}<-1/120000\) on \(|x|\le5\), so the second stationary set is empty there; the first contains only the origin, with a strictly positive Laguerre margin.
